newsitem.title: USA: What makes the perfect gift -- giving from the heart.
newsitem.headline: What makes the perfect gift -- giving from the heart.

text.p: Wondering what to do with the swiveling Elvis kitchen clock, flamingo lawn ornament or elephant motif picture frame that Santa put under the tree?
Chances are you'll put them in a special place -- a dark closet or the Goodwill bag.

Gift giving is perhaps the year's most anxiety-producing task. However, getting bad gifts comes in a close second, especially when the giver has no idea that they've given something so inappropriate or awful.
An Encino, Calif.-based tax professional has made a second career out of advising the gift-challenged on how to select gifts and what to do with the real losers one might receive.
Eva Rosenberg, dubbed the "bad gift terminator," got into the gift advice business because of her huge family.
"Basically, I hate shopping. In fact I can't find anything if I wanted to anyway," she said. She loves to give gifts, it's just the shopping that gets in the way.
Children are especially hard. "You give them stuff and they say, 'oh, thanks' or 'gee, you're so with it' when they really mean 'I'm way past that age.'"

If you take the direct route and ask a person what they want, it's unlikely you'll get a straight answer. Most often, people will give an ambiguous answer and be disappointed when the gift giving comes.

The only ones who often get what they want are brides who register for gifts in stores, or anyone else who leaves a detailed list of their wants. This might be the height of arrogance, Rosenberg said, but when you put what you want on a list, you'll save a lot of people a lot of grief.
The tried-and-true method for gift giving is to listen to what the person likes and give them what they would like to receive, not what you would like to receive.

Give amateur chefs some kitchen supplies, even if you're on a diet. Give a horsewoman a gift certificate to a riding shop, even if you're allergic. Give a teenager a rock CD, even if the music makes you sick.
When giving gifts at work, such as Secret Santa grab bags, get to know the person you're giving a gift to, or ask others about her, Rosenberg says.

Following this advice, one of Rosenberg's colleagues was a die-hard movie fan and she was given a gift certificate to a local cinema. Rosenberg advises spending an average of $10 to $20 on presents for business associates or co-workers.
Families are harder. "We're conditioned to tune out what they say... We talk to families but we don't really listen," she said.

Rosenberg suggests that when giving a family member a gift, try to personalize. Take, for example, Rosenbeg's rich aunt. After the death of the aunt's husband, Charlie, Rosenberg decided to give her aunt a "Charlie," and gifts each year were a Charlie Chan doll or Charlie Chaplin items.
Some of the best gifts for family members are those where you give a bit of yourself.

A romantic gift one partner could give another might be a voucher good for a private evening just for two. Couples might also give each other "control of the remote for a night" or a coupon worth a sink full of dirty dishes.
Children might consider giving their parents a voucher that says they will actually do what they're told for one day, or do two hours of babysitting for a younger sibling, or wash the family car.
Rosenberg likes to give her nieces and nephews a day of their own where they can to do anything they want alone with their aunt, such as a trip to Disneyland or Venice beach in Los Angeles.
What should you do when you get that horrible gift -- hot pink/lime green plaid pants or a jungle-print bath mat?

"Give it away if you feel it's a flat-out insult," Rosenberg said. Othewise, if the gift giver just doesn't have a clue what constitutes a good gift, teach them. Give this giver something they'll truly love. Sounds strange, Rosenberg admits, but it works.
"Some of the best ways to get nasty people (or those who give awful gifts) to your side is be nice and find great things," she said.
If someone gives you something they like, but it's not your taste, don't offend. Display the candle sticks when your friend visits and put them away as soon as they leave.
Here are some don'ts that Rosenberg advises for gift givers:
Don't give kitchen gifts to someone who doesn't cook. If you do, expect the juicer to sit unused, or be given to someone else.

Don't buy clothing, unless you know for sure exactly what the person wants. No matter what size you buy, it'll probably be too small. "And if you buy the person's real size, they're likely to be insulted because you think they're fat," she said.

Perfumes are another no no, unless, again, a brand is asked for. Many people may be allergic or have bad reactions. Some might think perfume is a "cop out" gift, given by someone too lazy to give something really meaningful.
Food is also a problem because many people have religious or cultural prohibitions. Avoid giving alcohol, because many people do not or should not drink.
But, Rosenberg said, almost everyone loves chocolate -- a never-fail winner in the gift category.

Rosenberg has established a Web site where gift recipients can post their preferences, My Wish List. http://www.mywishlist.com. She also edits a free newsletter for online gift shopping, GiftSurfer's Digest. To receive a free newsletter or to see it online, Rosenberg asks that you access the Web site.
You can write to Judith Schoolman at Reuters, 199 Water Street, 10th floor, N.Y., N.Y. 10038. Her e-mail address is Judith.Schoolman(at)reuters.com.
